Hi Amelia,

Thanks again for the time yesterday. Attached is a short packet with three reservation options we think map well to SapphireAI's initial production profile and anticipated growth over the next 9 months. High level:

- Option A — Minimal runway: 8 GPUs baseline, 2-week activation, burst up to +25% for 4 hours/day. Lower monthly commit; higher spot-like overage rates.
- Option B — Balanced commit: 24 GPUs baseline, staged ramp to 48 GPUs across 3 months, includes 40 hours/month burst credits and 5 pre-warm credits. Recommended for teams moving from proof-of-concept to production.
- Option C — Performance-first: 64 GPUs baseline, guaranteed lane isolation for latency-sensitive routes, on-call SLA and dedicated warm pool. Best for enterprise usage with strict latency SLOs.

I call out two items we often get asked about:
1) Minimum useful lane size — for Transformer-based chat workloads we typically see 8–12 GPUs as the realistic minimum to support decent concurrency without frequent eviction of warm KV caches.
2) Ramp schedule recommendations — customers often prefer a 3-stage ramp (pilot, steady-state, scale) with explicit burn-rate caps per stage so credits and commit hours are predictable.

Please see the attached PDF for a per-option cost/latency tradeoff and an activation checklist. Quick asks: could you confirm your expected 95th percentile concurrency and whether you expect most inference to be short chat (<512 tokens) or long-form generation (>=1500 tokens)? That will change the recommended kernel/quant profile and therefore the GPU sizing.

If the team prefers, we can also convert Option B into a 12-month staircase commit with quarterly step-ups.

Best,
Nikhil
Account Executive — Redwood Inference

Hi Amelia — thanks for the details, that helps. A few practical notes from product/ops: 

- Pre-warm credits are measured in "GPU-prewarm-hours." They are used to keep a small warm pool instantiated for your model variants (so KV caches and compiled kernels are hot). They do not represent "idle GPU time" you can consume for unrelated workloads; they're reserved specifically for warm-up and therefore reduce cold-start tail latency.

- For your traffic profile (120 -> 400 concurrent; mostly short), Option B with a steeper front-loaded ramp (24 -> 36 GPUs in month 1, then to 48 in month 3) tends to balance cost and tail latency. It gives you enough persistent KV cache capacity to avoid frequent cache eviction.

- Overage: when spikes are short (a few hours) per-day, hourly overage is usually predictable and simpler (you pay for dedicated GPU-hours above commit). Per-token bridging pricing can be better if spikes are token-heavy but sustained, because it scales with usage rather than reserved time. We can model both in the attached spreadsheet.

- Activation timeline: we can start warm pools within 7 business days of PO receipt for up to Option B; larger fleet activations (Option C) typically require 14–21 business days. We will include a staging window and test route for your team to smoke the endpoints.

I'm attaching an Ops checklist and minimal runbook fragment for the pilot activation.

-Ben
Senior Solutions Engineer — Redwood Inference

Hi Amelia — quick follow-up addressing procurement asks and flexibility: 

- Staircase step-downs: we can include one mid-year re-evaluation clause in a 12-month staircase allowing a single step-down (max 25% reduction) after Q2 review, provided usage and forecasting documentation is shared 30 days prior. - SLA credits: we propose a sliding-credit formula: 4% monthly credit for p95 latency breaches > 3x the committed baseline for more than 6 hours in a calendar month; 8% credit for sustained (>24 hours) severe degradation. We can map to 95th/99th as you need. The SLA_Addendum_Draft.docx attached includes language.
